## Sealed comparison (U57, U58) - Purpose: compare several published arms on one box under a design fixed before the run. Owner approval 2026-11-03 (contract gaps G1 comparison arms, G3 tolerance and equivalence, G6 compute metadata of the blind-02 science route); requirements from science steps s13 to s23. Arms are published programs or configurations that need no new code, run by the pipeline from sealed argument vectors. Each invocation runs one arm on one input, and invocations are interleaved on one box. No agent computes a number: every number comes from the pipeline's trusted wall time, from rules fixed before the run and applied by the pipeline, from a trusted comparator of two arms' outputs, or from a published evaluator that runs on each arm's output without access to the arm's identity. Criteria, margins, thresholds, reference values and timeouts are fixed by a science step before the run, sealed, and unreadable by the run's agents and by the processes of arms and evaluator. Compute is recorded twice and never mixed: per invocation as attribution and per box allocation as the bill. Never change a criterion after a result: every decision uses the sealed design. An outcome that is not supported is a result and never fails a stage. Comparisons that need more than one run are split by the science step into one design per run; a design whose launch depends on an earlier run's outcomes is launched only when the science step finds them in that run's `C/comparison_scored.json`. Without `args.comparison`, every stage is unchanged. Declared residual risks, which no rule below removes: the evaluator reads the arm's output files by design, so file names or content under `out/` that identify the program can reach it (the sealed `evaluate.sh` bytes make any dependence on them auditable after the run); state of shared hardware (device memory, caches, timing) is not cleared between parts; a harness script that disobeys the rule that only `fetch_private.sh` handles the evaluator's private data can leave a transformed copy of them (an archive, a re-encoding, a derived file) where the arm part can read it, which the byte-identity check of Separated users step 7 does not detect (`setup.sh` and its repairs are kept in `A/harness/` and the stage's receipts, so such a copy is auditable after the run); and processes, shell start-up hooks or scheduled jobs that `setup.sh`, its repairs or the anchors leave behind run as the box user, which the pipeline's own box commands also use, so they can read and change what the box user can (the same kept bytes make them auditable; the hash check of Separated users step 1 detects a sealed harness file changed before it). - Optional `args.comparison` is an object with exactly the key `design`: a non-empty path, resolved relative to the pipeline working directory, to a design JSON file. It is exclusive with `args.card`, `args.units_check` and `args.units_probe`. The design is exactly `{arms, inputs, outputs, metrics, evaluator, replicates, warmup, order_seed, timeout_s, budget_s, bootstrap_seed, bootstrap_resamples, comparisons}`: - `arms`: 2 to 5 items, each exactly `{id, what, commands, env}`; ids `"A0"`, `"A1"`, ... in order; `what` a non-empty string. `A0` is the published baseline that intake and reproduce handle as usual. - `commands`: 1 to 8 commands, each a non-empty array of non-empty strings: the exact published command lines of the arm, in order, as argument vectors run without a shell. The pipeline runs them (see Evaluate); the arm's adapter only prepares. - `env`: null or an object mapping names that match `^[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]{0,63}$` and do not start with `CMP_` to strings; set for the arm's commands. - Placeholders, in command and `env` strings only: `{input}` (the input id), `{run}`, `{out}` (the absolute paths of the invocation's `run/` and `out/`) and `{spec:

}` with `

` a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) into the input's `spec`, which must resolve in every input's `spec` to a string (inserted as is) or a finite number (inserted as `json.dumps` writes it). `{{` and `}}` stand for literal braces; any other `{` or `}` makes the design invalid. Substitution replaces every occurrence and is not repeated on its result. - `inputs`: 1 to 10 items, each exactly `{id, spec}`: `id` a unique string matching `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`; `spec` any JSON value (pins, case, configuration). - `outputs`: 0 to 10 items, each exactly `{name, what, format, select}`: a logical result each arm, or the evaluator, writes for an input, compared across arms. `name` unique, matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,30}$`; `what` a non-empty string; `format` `"bytes"`, `"text_numbers"` (every number in the file's UTF-8 text, in order, as matched by `[-+]?(\d+\.?\d*|\.\d+)([eE][-+]?\d+)?` together with `nan`, `inf` and `-inf` tokens) or `"json_numbers"` (every number leaf of the JSON document, in document order; booleans are not numbers). `select` is null (the whole content) or, for `bytes` and `text_numbers` only, a Python `re` pattern with at least one capturing group: the content is read as UTF-8 with replacement, and the selected content is every group of every match of `re.finditer(select, text, re.MULTILINE)`, in order (an unmatched group as the empty string), joined by `"\n"`; `format` then applies to the selected content (`bytes` to its UTF-8 encoding). Several outputs may select different parts of the same file, each with its own comparison and tolerance. - `metrics`: 1 to 10 items, each exactly `{name, unit, what, source, reduce, expect_count}`: `name` unique, matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,30}$`; `unit` and `what` non-empty strings; `source` `"trusted_wall"` or `"sealed_extraction"`. - `trusted_wall`: the invocation's wall seconds: the adapter's wall plus its commands' walls, plus the evaluator's wall when the design has an evaluator. `reduce` and `expect_count` are null. - `sealed_extraction`: read from fetched files by a rule the harness agent fixes before the run, reduced as the design states. `reduce` `"first"`, `"max"` or `"value_at_max_key"`; `expect_count` null or a positive integer, the number of matched values the rule must find. - `evaluator`: null or exactly `{what, spec, timeout_s}`: a published, pinned program that reads one arm's output for one input, with data that only it may read, and writes evaluation files. `what` a non-empty string; `spec` any JSON value (program, pin, command, and where its private data come from); `timeout_s` null or a positive integer. - `replicates` an integer from 1 to 30; `warmup` an integer from 0 to 3; `order_seed` and `bootstrap_seed` integers; `bootstrap_resamples` an integer from 1000 to 1000000; `budget_s` a positive integer, the evaluate stage's time budget for this comparison. When `args.run_ceiling_s` is present, `budget_s` must be below it. - `timeout_s`: null, a positive integer for every invocation, or an object mapping every arm id to a positive integer or to an object mapping every input id to a positive integer: the cap of one invocation's arm part. - `comparisons`: 0 to 12 items (0: a run that only records values and compute, for example to derive later reference values), each exactly `{id, arm, against, measure, criterion, direction, unit, pairing, rule, confidence, margin, threshold, strict, reference, missing, given, parts}`: - `id` unique, matching `^K[0-9]{1,2}$`; `arm` an arm id; `against` a different arm id or `"reference"`; `parts` a non-empty array of unique non-empty strings. - `measure` is exactly `{metric}` (a metric name) or exactly `{output, comparator}` (an output name and one of `"exact"`, `"elementwise_abs"`, `"elementwise_abs_plus_rel_max"`). An output comparison needs an arm as `against`. - `criterion` `"agreement"` (every output comparison and no metric comparison), `"non_inferiority"`, `"superiority"` or `"ratio_at_least"`. - `direction` `"higher_better"`, `"lower_better"` or `"two_sided"`: the metric as measured (for wall seconds, `lower_better`). `agreement` and `superiority` use `two_sided`; `non_inferiority` and `ratio_at_least` use `higher_better` or `lower_better`. - `unit` `"pooled_mean"` (each replicate's value is the mean over inputs, decided once), `"per_input_all"` (decided per input; the comparison holds only if it holds on every input) or `"per_input_each"` (decided and reported per input). - `pairing` `"paired_replicate"` or `"unpaired"`; `rule` `"all_pairs"` or `"bootstrap"`; `confidence` a number in `[0.5, 1)` for `bootstrap` and null for `all_pairs`. `ratio_at_least` uses exactly `pooled_mean`, `paired_replicate` and `bootstrap`; every other criterion uses `all_pairs` and a per-input unit; agreement uses `paired_replicate`. - `margin`: for an output comparison, the comparator's tolerance: null for `exact`, `{"abs": x}` for `elementwise_abs`, `{"abs": x, "rel": y}` for `elementwise_abs_plus_rel_max`. For `non_inferiority` and `superiority`, null or `{"abs": x}`. For `ratio_at_least`, null. `x` and `y` are finite and nonnegative. - `threshold`: a finite number above 0 for `ratio_at_least`, otherwise null. `strict`: a boolean for `ratio_at_least` (true: the bound must exceed `threshold`; false: it may equal it), otherwise null. - `reference`: exactly when `against` is `"reference"`, an object `{source, values}`: `source` a non-empty string naming where the values come from (for example an earlier run of this route and the rule that derived them), `values` mapping every input id to a finite number; otherwise null. A reference needs a metric `measure`, a per-input unit and `unpaired`. - `missing`: `"void"` or `"fail"`, how a missing value is decided (see Scoring). - `given`: an array, possibly empty, of unique ids of comparisons that come earlier in `comparisons`; a decision unit is decided only when each of them is supported for it (see Scoring). An invalid argument or design, or a path that cannot be read as JSON, fails intake with `error_class: parse` before any agent call. - Before the intake agent call and any box command, the pipeline writes atomically, in this order: `C/comparison.json`, exactly `{source, source_sha256, design}`; `C/comparison_seal.json`, exactly `{comparison_sha256, sealed_utc}` (the SHA-256 of the exact bytes of `C/comparison.json`); and `A/comparison_view.json`, exactly `{arms, inputs, outputs, metrics, evaluator, replicates, warmup}` copied from the design, with `evaluator` reduced to `{what, spec}` (null when the design's is null). The view holds no comparison, criterion, margin, threshold, reference value, timeout, part, seed or budget. Agents see only the view; comparison-mode prompts name it and never `C/` or the design path. The run root, the workflow journal directory and the design file must lie outside the pipeline working directory, which the isolation runner exposes to every agent call; otherwise intake fails with `error_class: parse` before any agent call. The science step that writes the design is responsible for the view's free text (`what`, `spec`, `select`) stating no expectation, criterion or result, and for keeping no copy of the design on the pipeline host outside the paths hidden below. - Isolation of agent calls, comparison mode only. Every agent call of the run (intake, harness, and every setup and anchors repair) is dispatched with wf `isolation` (see Implement) as implement's calls are: `directory` a fresh private view created for that call under the system temporary directory, `box_access` false, and `hidden` holding the run root, the workflow journal directory, the design file's parent directory and, when the design file lies inside a git work tree, that work tree's top-level directory (the nearest ancestor that contains `.git`). Under `isolation` the rest of the host is read-only and the view is the only writable host directory, so each role gets copies of what it reads today and writes only into its view; the pipeline copies its results back: - intake view: `comparison_view.json`; when the brief is a file, `brief/` (a copy of its bytes), which the prompt names in place of the brief's path; and an empty `intake/`. After the call the pipeline copies each regular file directly under the view's `intake/` (no symbolic link, no subdirectory) to `A/intake/`. - harness view: `comparison_view.json`, `intake/` (a copy of `A/intake/`) and an empty `harness/`; the probe stays in the prompt as today. After the call the pipeline copies each regular file directly under the view's `harness/`, and each regular file `harness/arms/.sh`, to the same name under `A/harness/`. - setup or anchors repair view: `comparison_view.json`, `intake/` and `harness/` (copies of `A/intake/` and `A/harness/`); the probe and log tail stay in the prompt. After the call the pipeline copies back only the scripts that repair may rewrite today (`setup.sh`; or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`), and discards every other change, as the existing restore of protected scripts does. When the view's `intake/`, `harness/` or `harness/arms/` is not a directory (a symbolic link included), nothing is copied from it, and no copy follows a symbolic link. Prompts name the view's paths in place of `A/intake/` and `A/harness/`. Network access is unchanged by `isolation`. A call that cannot be dispatched so fails as an isolation failure does; there is no fallback. Views are removed after the stage. - Intake prompt, comparison mode only: the run compares the view's arms on the view's inputs; `A0` is the benchmark intake records as usual; intake also records, in `benchmark.json` under the key `arms`, each other arm's published source, pin and commands, under the key `evaluator` the evaluator's published source, pin and command when the view has one, and in `data.json` every input any arm or the evaluator needs, marking the evaluator's private data and stating where each private item is published. - Harness prompt, comparison mode only: `setup.sh` also builds or installs every arm's published program and configuration, and the evaluator, as published, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. `setup.sh` never fetches, copies or writes the evaluator's private data; only `fetch_private.sh` does (see Separated users). CSV total time/duration units ns, us/µs, ms and s are converted to seconds. Known Nsight skips for absent kernel/memory/API activity count as zero; missing or malformed reports fail parsing. A report is a known skip when its CSV file carries Nsight's `SKIPPED` line and no header row, or when its CSV file is absent, empty or whitespace-only and `stats.log` in the same directory states that the report does not contain its own activity: `does not contain CUDA kernel data` for `stats_cuda_gpu_kern_sum.csv`, `does not contain GPU memory data` for `stats_cuda_gpu_mem_time_sum.csv`, and `does not contain CUDA trace data` for `stats_cuda_api_sum.csv` (U48). These are Nsight's own wordings; the earlier phrases `CUDA memory data` and `CUDA API data` never occur in Nsight output and no longer count as statements. Nsight Systems 2025 writes an empty file for a skipped report where earlier versions wrote none. An absent, empty or whitespace-only file without that statement for its own activity, and any other missing or malformed report, still fails parsing. Run evidence (blind-01 run9, 2026-11-01): the baseline ran to completion under the profiler with no CUDA activity and no capture problem; Nsight 2025 logged the three skips and wrote three empty summary files, and the summariser failed on a missing CSV header, so profile stopped with `parse` instead of reaching its numeric gate. Replay of the merged U48 summariser on run9's saved files (2026-11-01) still failed: Nsight states the memory and API skips as `GPU memory data` and `CUDA trace data`; with those wordings the summariser exits 0 and the gate reports `numeric` (other host time within 2% of total wall). Five rows are emitted: `kernels` (compute), `memcpy H2D` (transfer), `memcpy D2H` (transfer), `CUDA API host time` (other), and `other host time` (other). GPU seconds retain the raw kernel/transfer sums; host GPU seconds are null. Aggregate CSV reports do not identify critical-path intervals: if the four reported sums exceed measured wall, their wall allocations are scaled proportionally to fit. Other host time is the nonnegative wall remainder. These allocations are an aggregate approximation, not measured exclusive phase durations. No stage timestamps are invented; aggregate rows omit `start_s`, so stage utilisation remains null. No bound uses stage utilisation; same-GPU headroom comes from the concurrency probe. - `stages.json` is an array of `{stage, wall_s, gpu_s}`, optionally including `kind`: `compute`, `transfer`, or `other`, and `start_s`: finite nonnegative elapsed seconds sharing the telemetry clock. Fixed profiler supplies `kind`; legacy rows without it remain accepted. `stage` is a non-empty string; `wall_s` is finite nonnegative seconds; `gpu_s` is finite nonnegative seconds or null and must be present. Fixed profiler wall allocations sum to measured wall without exceeding it; overlapping aggregate durations use the approximation above. Extra input fields are not copied to the packet. Empty arrays parse but fail the numeric gate. - `total_wall_s.json` is an object with finite positive numeric `total_wall_s` in seconds. The sum of stage wall times must also be finite. - `gpu_util.json` is an array of `{t, util}` samples collected with `nvidia-smi` during the measured run. `t` is finite nonnegative elapsed seconds; `util` is a finite GPU utilisation percentage in [0,100]. The fixed sampler records the mean across GPUs returned by nvidia-smi, then the summarizer retains only samples during the shared command and rebases monotonic timestamps to its start. A sample with zero utilisation is valid. Empty arrays parse but fail the numeric gate; missing files or malformed samples fail parsing. - The deterministic pipeline writes `A/profile-packet.json` with exact keys: - `stages`: the validated timing rows, preserving optional `kind`, each augmented with `wall_fraction = min(1, wall_s / total_wall_s)`, `start_s`, and `mean_gpu_util` (fraction in [0,1], or null). When supplied, `start_s` must be measured on the telemetry clock. Legacy rows without `start_s` record null start and utilisation; stage order does not establish a measured telemetry window. Stage endpoints must remain finite. Stage utilisation is the arithmetic mean of telemetry percentages divided by 100 in `[start_s, start_s + wall_s)`; no samples means null. Never substitute GPU busy seconds for utilisation;

Can MEGADOCK’s GPU implementation make denser docking search affordable, and does that improve pose recovery within a fixed budget?

Use the four unbound PINDER cases examined by blind01’s unit probe. Pin their exact identities, prepared inputs and reference structures before execution. Treat this as a small pilot.

Compare three configurations:

1. CPU execution with standard rotational sampling.
2. GPU execution with the same sampling and scientific settings.
3. GPU execution with the documented denser rotational sampling.

Use MEGADOCK’s existing implementations. Keep scoring settings and the number of retained predictions fixed at 50.

First establish correct execution and scientific agreement between CPU and GPU configurations at identical search settings. Define justified numerical tolerances before examining comparative results.

Then measure whether denser search improves recovery. Report DockQ for the top-ranked prediction and the best of 50 separately. Use reference structures only for evaluation.

Use a small runtime calibration to define feasible budgets. Seal configurations, timing repetitions, comparison rules and the total spending cap before evaluation. Report complete workflow time, GPU activity and billed allocation cost.

Keep three conclusions separate: execution acceleration, scientific agreement at identical settings, and quality changes from additional search. Preserve negative results and budget overruns.

Identify any pipeline contract that cannot express these comparisons. Report that limitation explicitly without substituting a different scientific question.

Limit conclusions to these four cases. Do not infer biological efficacy from docking accuracy.

## Comparison request (science step s28)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, fixture inputs, outputs and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is a recording run on fixture inputs, repeating an earlier recording run of this route with two corrections to how the programs are built and invoked (GPU build target, evaluator invocation). It is not the seed's main experiment, and the seed's four cases above are not run, fetched or evaluated in it. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Four arms, as the view describes them. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1). A1 is the seed's configuration 2. A2 repeats A0's commands and A3 repeats A1's commands, each as separate invocations. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four fixture inputs, as the view describes them: holo test-set monomer pairs of four PINDER `2024-02` systems that are not among the seed's four cases. Each input's `spec` names its receptor and ligand sources (URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, and its native complex, which only the evaluator may read.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Fixture inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec`, checks the byte count and SHA-256 recorded there (any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the chain field (column 22) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It records the SHA-256 of every prepared file in its setup record.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation (correction): BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. The evaluator's Python code is therefore also kept as a regular file in `harness/` (for example `harness/evaluate_dockq.py`, uploaded with the harness) and run as `"$VPY" <that file>` by `evaluate.sh`, never as `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program.
- `cmp_files.json`: `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 and A2 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A3 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).

Boundaries

- No agent, adapter or harness script computes, prints or asserts any difference between arms, any tolerance or any summary of DockQ values. The pipeline records and compares the outputs.
- Preserve every invocation's files, failures and timeouts as they are. Do not rerun any invocation outside the pipeline's schedule.
- If intake or the harness cannot express this run within these boundaries, report the exact contract gap and stop before paid work.

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, fixture inputs, outputs and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is a recording run on fixture inputs, repeating an earlier recording run of this route with two corrections to how the programs are built and invoked (GPU build target, evaluator invocation). What the run does

- Four arms, as the view describes them. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1). A1 is the seed's configuration 2. A2 repeats A0's commands and A3 repeats A1's commands, each as separate invocations. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four fixture inputs, as the view describes them: holo test-set monomer pairs of four PINDER `2024-02` systems that are not among the seed's four cases. Each input's `spec` names its receptor and ligand sources (URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, and its native complex, which only the evaluator may read.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Fixture inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec`, checks the byte count and SHA-256 recorded there (any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the chain field (column 22) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. ## Comparison request (science step s28)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, fixture inputs, outputs and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is a recording run on fixture inputs, repeating an earlier recording run of this route with two corrections to how the programs are built and invoked (GPU build target, evaluator invocation). It is not the seed's main experiment, and the seed's four cases above are not run, fetched or evaluated in it. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Four arms, as the view describes them. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1). A1 is the seed's configuration 2. A2 repeats A0's commands and A3 repeats A1's commands, each as separate invocations. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four fixture inputs, as the view describes them: holo test-set monomer pairs of four PINDER `2024-02` systems that are not among the seed's four cases. Each input's `spec` names its receptor and ligand sources (URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, and its native complex, which only the evaluator may read.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Fixture inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec`, checks the byte count and SHA-256 recorded there (any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the chain field (column 22) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It records the SHA-256 of every prepared file in its setup record.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation (correction): BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. The evaluator's Python code is therefore also kept as a regular file in `harness/` (for example `harness/evaluate_dockq.py`, uploaded with the harness) and run as `"$VPY" <that file>` by `evaluate.sh`, never as `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program.

# s28 assessment: fixture run run7 against s27's sealed rule (2026-11-04)

**Scope.** Offline step: no network, no box, no git, no credentials. Bash was denied after its first call, so I read with the file tools and wrote with the file tool. I hashed nothing and compared bytes only by reading. I wrote only into `science/s28/`.
- **Read:** s27 (assessment, `TOLERANCE_RULE.md`, `tolerance_rule.json`, `fixture_design.json`, `PREDICTIONS.md`, `FIXTURE_BRIEF.md`) and s26 §A. I did not reread s01 to s25 in this step; s27 summarizes what they establish.
- **Contract:** `dut/pipeline/m5/SCHEMAS.md:115-203`.
- **run7:** `control/` (seal, scored file, evaluate stage, receipts 0009-0037), `agent/results/evaluate/comparison_compute.json`, `agent/harness/evaluate.sh`, `agent/harness/setup.sh`, the operator takeaway, and a selected handful of fetched files.
- **Seed outputs:** none read. run7 never ran the seed cases.

**Verdict.**
- **What run7 recorded:** no scored data. A harness defect in the evaluator part, not invocation cost, ate the budget. All 13 invocations that ran belonged to the warmup round.
- **The rule:** s27's rule applies and gives **indefensible** for M2 to M6 (reason `fixture_incomplete`). M1's flags are empty.
- **Next test:** a corrected fixture rerun (m5), which is justified and fits the limits.

## A. What run7 recorded

**Schedule.**
- The design asked for 7 rounds (1 warmup + 6 replicates) × 4 arms × 4 fixtures = 112 invocations.
- `comparison_compute.json` lists those 112 rows. 13 have status `ok` and 99 are `not_run` (rows at lines 3-171 against 172-1458).
- All 13 executed invocations are in the **warmup** round. Their fetched folders are `agent/results/evaluate/comparison/w1/<arm>/<input>/`, and no `r<r>` folder exists.
- So no replicate invocation ran.

**The 13 invocations,** in run order (`comparison_compute.json:3-171`; walls in s). Every evaluator part has `eval_status` `timeout`; the eval wall is 901.0 for each, except invocation 13, which is noted in its row.

| k | arm | input | arm wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A2 | f1glj | 19.98 |
| 2 | A0 | f1glj | 19.93 |
| 3 | A1 | f1a19 | 1.60 |
| 4 | A0 | f1ht8 | 39.05 |
| 5 | A1 | f1dtd | 2.37 |
| 6 | A0 | f1dtd | 9.79 |
| 7 | A2 | f1dtd | 9.79 |
| 8 | A1 | f1ht8 | 6.43 |
| 9 | A1 | f1glj | 3.32 |
| 10 | A2 | f1a19 | 2.52 |
| 11 | A3 | f1ht8 | 6.43 |
| 12 | A3 | f1glj | 3.27 |
| 13 | A2 | f1ht8 | 22.04 (eval wall 665.79, cut at the budget) |

**Coverage.**
- **By arm:** A0 3, A1 4, A2 4, A3 2.
- **Missing from the warmup round:** A0 f1a19, A1 f1glj (an A1 f1glj did run), A3 f1a19 and A3 f1dtd. Precisely, the remaining warmup pairs were not reached.

**Which outputs have values.**
- Every executed invocation has `out/docking.out` and `out/model_1..50.pdb`; for example, `w1/A1/f1a19/out/`. Every arm command's `rc` is 0 (`w1/A1/f1a19/wrap.json:34,48`).
- No `eval/` folder holds a `dockq.json`. Each holds only `evaluator.log`.
- Warmup rounds are not scored (`SCHEMAS.md:190`), so `comparison_scored.json` has 0 present pairs in all 12 comparisons × 4 fixtures, and every unit is void with reason `missing_values`.
- Totals: supported 0, not_supported 0, inconclusive 0, void 48 (`comparison_scored.json:2861-2865`).
- The seal matches: `comparison_sha256` `c42b95cb…` in both `comparison_scored.json:2` and `comparison_seal.json:2`. Evaluate is PASS (`control/stages/evaluate.json`).

**Parts' walls against the comparison receipts.** Each `comparison` receipt minus the invocation's arm and eval walls gives the overhead of the wrapper, cleanups and fetch:

| receipt | wall | arm + eval walls | overhead |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0012 | 961 | 921.0 | 40 |
| 0014 | 964 | 921.0 | 43 |
| 0016 | 945 | 902.6 | 42 |
| 0018 | 989 | 940.1 | 49 |
| 0036 | 732 | 687.8 | 44 |

- Each `comparison-job` receipt took 23 to 31 s (for example `0013-comparison-job.json`: 23 s).
- **Fixed cost per invocation outside the parts:** about 63 to 80 s, against s27's assumed ~30 s.
- **Other evaluate-stage commands:** users 49 s (`0009`); `comparison-private-remove` 23 s (`0037`).

**Why it covered what it did.** The evaluator part hung on every invocation until its 900 s cap.
- `evaluate.sh:11` runs the evaluator as `"$VPY" - <<'PY'` (Python code read from standard input).
- `BiotiteDockQ` defaults to `parallel_io=True` (`pinder/eval/dockq/biotite_dockq.py:226`, in the fetched venv), which calls `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Pool` (`pinder/core/utils/process.py:17,33`).
- Spawned workers re-import the main module from its path, and the path is `<stdin>`. Every worker dies with `FileNotFoundError: … '/tmp/m5-…/<stdin>'` (`w1/A1/f1a19/eval/evaluator.log:1-15`, repeated), and the pool waits forever.
- **Cost:** about 13 × (901 + ~70) s ≈ 12,600 s, the whole `budget_s`. The evaluate stage took 12,695 s against 12,600 s.
- **Not the cause: the box.** The arm parts took 1.6 to 39 s. On an H100 the evaluator would have hung the same way.
- **Not the cause: a real per-invocation cost.** run4 measured complete 50-model evaluations at no more than 2.573 s (`s26/ASSESSMENT.md:38`).
